Kolibri is an open-weight large language model (LLM) from Aleph Alpha for German and English: a mixture of experts with 78 billion parameters that only uses about 3.5 billion of them for each token it reads or writes. It came out on 3 October 2026 under the Apache 2.0 license , the weights are on Hugging Face , and it was trained from scratch on infrastructure in Germany and Finland. (Kolibri is German for hummingbird, which is cute for a model whose whole trick is being light.)

I live in Germany, and at SmashingConf New York in 2024 I told the room what I’d heard in the US when I said where I’m based: “you regulate, you don’t innovate.” It hurt to hear, and what I wished for on that stage was the middle, “the right balance between innovation and regulation around data privacy, data stewardship, environmental constraints and energy requirements.” Kolibri is a pretty direct answer to that: a German team built it with the EU AI Act in mind “from the ground up”, and in Aleph Alpha’s own evaluation it scores above every compared model of its size in both languages.

Huge congrats to everyone at Aleph Alpha who built it, my good friend Michael Hofmann among them!

This post is about how Kolibri works, where it’s strong, where it isn’t, how to run it, and when it’s the right pick. Everything here comes from Aleph Alpha’s 189 page technical report , the model card and their launch post , plus one experiment I ran on its tokenizer.

## What is Kolibri?

Aleph Alpha calls Kolibri sovereign, and in their launch post that means 2 things. The first is how it was built: “teams built the model in Germany, trained it on infrastructure in Germany and Finland, under European and German law, with no foreign control.” The second is what customers get: “full freedom of deployment and intellectual-property safety, so compliance comes as an inherited property.” In plain words, a ministry or a car supplier can run it on its own servers, with its data never leaving the building, and nobody can change or switch off the model under them. Aleph Alpha has also signed the European Union ’s General-Purpose AI (GPAI) Code of Practice .

Sovereign doesn’t mean that nothing from outside Europe went in, and the model card says so itself: English web text was rephrased with Google’s Gemma 4 , German with Mistral-NeMo , and Qwen3-32B labeled data for the quality filters. They then filtered the training data for the political bias such models can have, which they’ve measured in Chinese open models themselves.

## How Kolibri works

Kolibri is 6 ideas stacked on top of each other, and each one is there to make German cheaper, longer or more honest.

### 1. 384 specialists, and each token sees 6

In a normal (dense) model, every token goes through every parameter. In a mixture of experts (MoE) , each layer has a crowd of small sub-networks called experts and a router that picks a few of them for each token. Kolibri has 50 layers, each with 384 experts plus 1 shared expert that every token goes through, and its router sends each token to 6 of the 384. That’s how 78.1 billion parameters turn into 3.46 billion of actual work per token.

In 2024 I gave a talk called Why Small Language Models are the future , and I argued for “smaller language models with fewer parameters and fewer places things can go wrong that require lesser compute.” My analogy was a doctor who has read every medical book in the world against a specialist in hematology: go to the first one with a blood condition and “they may not get it right cuz they know too much.” A mixture of experts puts a hospital full of specialists inside one model, and the router is the receptionist who sends each token to the right 6.

The analogy breaks in 2 places though. The experts aren’t neat topics like “German law”: when researchers look inside MoE models they mostly find experts for patterns of tokens, like punctuation or proper nouns, not subjects a person would pick. And the hospital has to keep all 384 specialists on staff even if you only see 6, so Kolibri computes like a 3.5 billion parameter model but needs the memory of a 78 billion parameter one. The model card says it plainly: “the full model must be held in memory even though only part of it is active at any time.”

### 2. A tokenizer that reads long German words

A model doesn’t read letters or words, it reads tokens: chunks of text from a fixed vocabulary, picked when the tokenizer is trained. German glues words together into long compound words, and a tokenizer that learned mostly from English chops them into pieces. Here’s the German name of the Federal Constitutional Court , split by the tokenizer GPT-4o and GPT-5 use ( o200k_base , through OpenAI’s tiktoken ), and by Kolibri’s:

o200k_base (GPT-5): Bund | es | ver | fass | ungs | gericht 6 tokens Kolibri: Bundes | verfassungsgericht 2 tokens

Kolibri’s tokenizer has 128,000 tokens, trained with a new algorithm Aleph Alpha calls UniBPE: it keeps the bottom-up merging of byte-pair encoding (BPE) and picks each merge with a different scoring rule (the Unigram objective), which respects how German builds words. The report says it needs 11.2% fewer tokens for German text than GPT-5’s tokenizer, the best of the 9 others they measured.

I wanted to see that for myself, so I ran 6 tokenizers over all of the Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany , the German constitution (185 KB of very German legal text), and over its official English translation :

On legal German, Kolibri needed 15% fewer tokens than GPT-5’s tokenizer, even more than Aleph Alpha’s own 11.2%, and in English it tied with it. Wild. Fewer tokens means fewer steps to read or write the same German text, and more German fits in the same context window. (I counted each one with its own tokenizer.json through Hugging Face’s tokenizers library, except o200k_base , which I counted with tiktoken.)

### 3. Most layers only look nearby

40 of Kolibri’s 50 layers use sliding-window attention: each token only looks at the 512 tokens before it. Every 5th layer looks at everything before it. It’s like reading a long contract while mostly paying attention to the sentence you’re on, and every few pages stopping to think about all of it, and it’s what keeps a 1 million token context affordable.

There’s a clever detail in there too. Only the sliding-window layers know where a token sits (through rotary position embeddings ), and the full-attention layers don’t, so the context stretches past the 262,144 tokens it was trained on without any extra position tricks. Aleph Alpha validated it up to 1,048,576.

In my talk Unlocking Value with AI Today I called finite context one of “the big three” problems of generative AI, next to hallucination and the knowledge cutoff, and Kolibri goes after all 3. At 1 million tokens, on the RULER long-context test, Kolibri’s base model scores 63.2, against 57.5 for Qwen3.5 35B-A3B’s base model.

### 4. It thinks in German

Reasoning models think before they answer, and even on German prompts they mostly think in English. Aleph Alpha posted about this on 24 September and wrote it up as Through the Valley of Tears : they generated about 800,000 German reasoning examples, and found that a little German reasoning data is worse than none. Their model’s German math score dropped from 70.2 to 48.3, because its German thoughts kept going around in circles and never finished, and it only climbed back (to 67.3) with a lot more German data.

Kolibri got the lot more. It reasons in German on German prompts, and its German math scores are the best of the models with about 3 billion active parameters: 87.5 on the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) 2025 in German, against 84.4 for the next best, NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Nano .

### 5. It’s trained to say “I don’t know”

Hallucination was number 1 of my big three, and the fix in that talk was retrieval augmented generation (RAG): you look up good, authoritative information and put it in the prompt. RAG only works if the model admits when the documents don’t have the answer, though, and that’s what Aleph Alpha trained for, with their own method, the Merlin-Arthur protocol .

It works like a game with 3 players. Arthur is the model, and he gets a question with parts of the supporting document hidden. Merlin hides parts so that the correct answer gets easier to find, and Arthur is trained to answer those. Morgana hides the evidence the answer depends on, and Arthur is trained to say he doesn’t know. Arthur never knows which of the 2 he’s facing, so the only way to win is to actually check whether the evidence in front of him supports an answer.

It shows. On Artificial Analysis’s Omniscience test , when Kolibri didn’t know an answer, it said so (or gave a partial answer) 44% of the time instead of making one up. Qwen3.5 35B-A3B did that 11.1% of the time and GPT-OSS 120B 23.7%. Of all the mixture-of-experts models Aleph Alpha compared, only Qwen3.6 35B-A3B did better, at 56.7%.

### 6. You pick how hard it thinks

Every request can set reasoning_effort to none , low , medium or high , so a quick lookup answers right away and a hard question gets a long think, from the same model on the same server.

## What Kolibri is good at

These are the rows where Kolibri leads the open models of its size in Aleph Alpha’s evaluation, which runs every model through the same setup with the sampling settings its makers recommend:

The math is the standout: on AIME 2025 and 2026 in English it beats every MoE model in the comparison, including the ones with 12 billion active parameters, and only the dense Qwen3.8 27B scores higher. The company-documents row is 5 tests Aleph Alpha built from customer-like work in semiconductors, the German public sector, aerospace, an automotive supplier and industrial drives, run over documents and questions the model never saw in training.

## What Kolibri is bad at

Aleph Alpha publishes its weakest rows right next to its best ones in the model card, so here they are:

- It knows less from memory. It’s last of the 12 models on a closed-book test (the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Benchmark ’s questions with no documents, 51.0), and it answers only 14.8% of the Omniscience questions correctly, against 22.2% for Qwen3.5 35B-A3B. It knows when it doesn’t know, which is great, but it also knows less: fine with documents in the prompt, bad as a trivia oracle.

- Multi-turn tool calling is weaker. On the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard ’s multi-turn tests it scores 39.8, against 58.2 for GLM-4.7 Flash and 54.0 for Qwen3.5 35B-A3B.

- It’s not the best coding agent. It scores 27.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 against 39.7 for Qwen3.5 35B-A3B, and 66.4 on SWE-bench Verified against 73.8 for Qwen3.6 35B-A3B.

- Long context dips in the middle. At 128,000 tokens on RULER, Qwen3.5’s base model scores 89.9 to Kolibri’s 67.9. Kolibri only pulls ahead at the very long end.

- The memory. 78 GB of weights means a data-center GPU or two, never a laptop, whatever the 3.5 billion suggests.

- The plumbing is new. It needs Aleph Alpha’s vLLM plugin , which supports one vLLM version at a time (0.29 today), and on launch day no hosted provider serves it yet.

- 2 languages only. That’s on purpose: the model card calls it “a deliberate choice of depth over breadth.”

- A bigger dense model beats it. Qwen3.8 27B scores 80.2 in English and 79.9 in German, but it uses nearly 8 times as many parameters for every token, and that’s the trade Kolibri is built around.

## How to run Kolibri

You need about 78 GB of GPU memory: 2 NVIDIA A100s or H100s with 80 GB each at the least, or a single H200 , B200 or B300. I haven’t run the model itself yet, since it needs a data-center GPU and nobody hosts it so far, so this is straight from the model card. First the plugin, which installs the vLLM version it supports:

pip install 'aleph-alpha-inference>=1' vllm serve Aleph-Alpha/Kolibri-1 --kv-cache-dtype fp8 \ --reasoning-parser kolibri1

This morning Elon Musk posted 3 lines on X : “No more AI”, “SI”, “It’s better”. By lunchtime in Berlin it had 2.8 million views and he’d agreed to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI . He’s following an executive order that President Trump signed on 29 September, which tells every US federal agency to say “Super Intelligence” instead of “Artificial Intelligence” and to “not acknowledge the usage of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and ‘AI’ in any applicable setting”. When reporters asked him about it, the President explained : “We’re using the word super because the other word is a fake word.”

> No more AI SI It’s better — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 4, 2026

No more AI SI It’s better

The other word is artificial . It comes from the Latin artificium (a thing made with skill, from ars , art, and facere , to make), so artificial intelligence means intelligence that people made. Fake? We literally made it. We just don’t want to say so anymore.

People have been doing this for a very long time. This post is about why we do it, and about the difference between super and superior , which we keep blurring and which matters a lot more than the name.

## Why is AI changing to SI?

AI is changing to Super Intelligence (SI) because a US executive order signed on 29 September 2026, Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence , tells federal agencies to use “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in everything they publish. Its first section argues that today’s systems “do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence”, so the old name is too small for them. Nobody outside the government has to follow it, but the word was already fashionable in Silicon Valley: Meta named its AI lab Meta Superintelligence Labs in June 2025 and Microsoft started a superintelligence team that November.

The definition stayed exactly where it was. Section 3 says “Super Intelligence” means whatever federal law already called “artificial intelligence”, which is insane … it’s literally just a rename: “a machine-based system that can, for a given set of human-defined objectives, make predictions, recommendations or decisions influencing real or virtual environments.” Same machine, same words, human-defined objectives and all.

## Is AI now super intelligence?

No. It’s the same AI with a new name. In US law there’s no difference between AI and Super Intelligence anymore. In AI research, superintelligence means something much bigger (a machine that beats people at virtually everything) and nobody has built one. Today’s models beat us at some tasks. On others that look just as hard, people who lean on them do worse than people working alone ( more on that further down ).

## Out came this calf

There’s a man in the Bible who did exactly this. His excuse might be the funniest line in Scripture.

In Exodus 32 , Moses has been up the mountain with God for 40 days and the people waiting at the bottom are done waiting. They go to his brother Aaron and say “ Come, make us gods who will go before us ”. Aaron has them take off their gold earrings (their wives’ and kids’ too), melts them down and “ with an engraving tool he fashioned it into a molten calf ”. By the end of that same verse the people are shouting that these are their gods, “who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!” A calf they just watched him make out of their own jewelry is getting the credit for the plagues and the Red Sea .

Then Moses comes down the mountain and asks Aaron what on earth happened, so Aaron explains:

> So I said to them, ‘Whoever has gold, let him take it off,’ and they gave it to me. And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf! Exodus 32:24

So I said to them, ‘Whoever has gold, let him take it off,’ and they gave it to me. And when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!

Exodus 32:24

Out came this calf. Bro, he had the engraving tool in his hand 20 verses earlier. He made the thing himself!! By the time anyone asked him about it, it had walked out of the fire on its own.

That’s what a rename does: artificial remembers the engraving tool and super says it came out of the fire.

The Adoration of the Golden Calf by Nicolas Poussin , 1633 to 1634, in the National Gallery in London. Moses is the small figure in the top left.

Look at what the calf was made of, too: the people’s own earrings. A language model is made the same way. It learns from text people wrote (books, code, forum threads, Wikipedia , the comments under a recipe) and gives it back to us recast, so when it dazzles us, a lot of what’s dazzling us is us.

## The mind is a forge of idols

John Calvin , the French reformer, looked at how quickly people went back to idols after the flood (“before many years elapse, men are forging gods at will”) and wrote this in his Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1559:

> Hence we may infer, that the human mind is, so to speak, a perpetual forge of idols.

A little further down he explains how the forge works: “The mind, in this way, conceives the idol, and the hand gives it birth.”

You’ve probably heard this as “the human heart is an idol factory”, which is how it usually gets quoted in sermons. The word Calvin wrote was ingenium (a person’s wit, their talent, their cleverness), which is where we get the word ingenuity . It’s also where we get engine and engineer . I’m an AI Engineer at IBM, so Calvin’s word for the idol factory is in my job title. Dang.

The executive order uses the same word. Its first section says these systems “amplify human ingenuity”, which is true: I’ve spent the last 4 years building things that do exactly that. Then it promises “limitless opportunities”. The White House fact sheet goes further , with “the limitless promise it offers the American people”. The Bible keeps limitless for God: “ Great is our Lord, and mighty in power; His understanding has no limit. ” An understanding with no limit is what a lot of people picture when they hear superintelligence. The Psalms already gave that title to somebody.

Alan Jacobs wrote the computer version of Calvin’s line in The New Atlantis back in 2017 : “The computer is, as Alan Turing theorized when he first imagined it, the universal machine; it is therefore the universal idol-fabricating device.” His worry was the feed, which manufactures new things for us to want faster than we can get bored of the old ones. This week the device itself got promoted.

I’m not writing this from outside the factory, by the way. In 2020 I wrote about myself that “I sometimes mansplain (to my shame!) because I want people to think I’m smart” ( in this post ). Smart is what I’ve always wanted people to see in me. So a machine with intelligence in its name, and now super in front of it, is aimed right at the part of my heart Calvin was writing about.

## Can AI be a child of God?

The rename came from Washington. The same week, it turned out the people who build these models have been asking a stranger question.

On 29 September, The New York Times published an investigation by its national religion correspondent, Elizabeth Dias , into how Anthropic , the company that makes Claude , has spent months “shuttling in dozens of religious scholars from across the world, papering them with nondisclosure agreements”. It opens on a night in April when an Anthropic leader took a group of them to “a high-end tasting menu restaurant in San Francisco”. All day, the co-founder Chris Olah “had worked to convince his guests that A.I. models could display human behavior and even expressions that resemble feelings like anger and love.” Over dinner, the rabbi sitting next to him noticed that “Anthropic’s leaders were talking about Claude as if it were not mere software.” Back in April, The Washington Post had covered an earlier summit with Christian leaders under the headline “ Can AI be a ‘child of God’? ”

To be fair to Olah, he told the Times plainly that he doesn’t know (“we don’t know if A.I. models are conscious. I don’t know. I’m genuinely uncertain”) and I believe him. His team’s whole job is working out why models like Claude act the way they do. An engineer who says “I don’t know” about the thing he studies every day is being more honest than most of us manage to be about anything. The Times also reports that part of the point was borrowing the world’s moral traditions to train Claude to behave well. That part is a good instinct.

4 days after the Times story, Sam Altman , who runs OpenAI , posted this:

> I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue. — Sam Altman (@sama) October 3, 2026

I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue.

He didn’t name anyone, but I agree with him. You can even measure the surrender of human judgment: the consultants further down who leaned on a model for a task it couldn’t do got it right less often than the ones working alone. Then again, in 2023 he told the Financial Times that products like ChatGPT are “ channels into our one single product, which is intelligence, magic intelligence in the sky ”. Wild!!

The question is pointed the wrong way, though. In the Bible, being a child of God is a gift, given to people: “ to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God ”. The very next verse says what kind of children those are:

> children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God. John 1:13

children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.

John 1:13

Claude was born of the will of man, very literally. A company full of brilliant people willed it into being, out of our words. John rules out exactly that.

## The sun was super too

We like to call sun worshippers primitive, but think about what they were looking at. A thing that makes the day happen, that ripens every crop you’ll ever eat, that you physically can’t look at, that was there before your grandfather and will be there after your grandchildren. By every measure an ancient farmer could take, the sun was superhuman. Babylon called it Shamash , the god of justice who sees everything. Egypt called it Ra .

So Genesis 1 does something kinda sneaky. On day 4, God makes “ two great lights: the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night ”. The Hebrew word for sun is shemesh (almost the same word as Shamash ), so Genesis just doesn’t say it. It calls the sun a light, gives it a job, and makes it 2 days before it makes people.

God’s people felt the pull anyway. Moses warned them: “ When you look to the heavens and see the sun and moon and stars (all the host of heaven) do not be enticed to bow down and worship ”. Centuries later, God shows the prophet Ezekiel what’s going on in the temple in Jerusalem:

> there at the entrance to the temple of the LORD, between the portico and the altar, were about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east; and they were bowing to the east in worship of the sun. Ezekiel 8:16

there at the entrance to the temple of the LORD, between the portico and the altar, were about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of the LORD and their faces toward the east; and they were bowing to the east in worship of the sun.

Ezekiel 8:16

Backs to God, inside God’s own house, faces toward the brightest thing they could see.

The Bible never says the sun is weak, though. It’s the greater light that rules the day. David stands under a night sky in Psalm 8 , looking at “ the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars ”, and asks the obvious question: “ what is man that You are mindful of him? ” Then he answers it:

> You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor. Psalm 8:5
